items.title: In Interview, Sonia Gandhi Recalls Love and Loss in India
items.summary: In a new memoir and interview, the Italian-born woman who married into the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty recalls her political battles and the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law.
items.full_text:
Title: In Interview, Sonia Gandhi Recalls Love and Loss in India - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world/asia/sonia-gandhi-india.html

Published Time: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 08:32:48 GMT

Markdown Content:
The astonishing story of Sonia Gandhi, the young woman from a middle-class Italian family who married into the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty, lived through unspeakable tragedy and nearly became prime minister of India, reached a crescendo in May 2004 in her heavily fortified home in New Delhi.

“It took place in this very room,” she said in an interview last week in her home office, once that of her late husband, Rajiv Gandhi.

His tricolor Congress Party shawl still hung over his desk chair in the corner, where it has been since his assassination in 1991, when he was campaigning to be prime minister a second time. On the wall was a photograph of Jawaharlal Nehru, Rajiv’s grandfather and India’s first prime minister, and another of Rajiv’s mother, Indira Gandhi, who was assassinated as prime minister less than seven years before her son.

On that day in 2004, party elders beseeched Sonia Gandhi, criticized by the opposition as a foreign-born interloper, to take her place as prime minister as the leader of the Congress Party, which had just won national elections. She initially said yes, horrifying her two children, Rahul and Priyanka, but recanted.

“My brother and I actually thought that she would get killed, too,” said Priyanka Gandhi, who sat next to her mother in the interview.

Image

![Image 1: Two women in red saris are in a room with a framed black-and-white photograph of Mahatma Gandhi. ](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/10/multimedia/10int-sonia-gandhi-03-gkwb/10int-sonia-gandhi-03-gkwb-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Sonia Gandhi with her daughter, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, a member of Parliament, at their New Delhi home, where a portrait of Mahatma Gandhi is displayed. Credit...Saumya Khandelwal for The New York Times

And yet today Rahul Gandhi, 56, the current leader of India’s largest opposition party, is putting himself at risk as he has risen from the political sidelines to stand with the massive youth protests against the Hindu nationalist government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. “It does worry me,” said Sonia Gandhi, 79, who said she feared for the safety of her children, both now members of the lower house of India’s Parliament.

But she said she was never afraid that she herself might die in the years when she led the Congress Party after her husband’s death. “Maybe subconsciously, I really didn’t care if it happened,” she said.

Sonia Gandhi has just published a sprawling, highly personal and at times harrowing memoir, “Belonging: A Journey of Love,” that evokes a politics of martyrdom rather than ambition in her years leading the Congress Party. She is critical of Mr. Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, which she said in the interview has “destroyed” the secular Indian democracy that her family has long stood for, if not always practiced.

The deeply entrenched B.J.P. has dismissed the book as political propaganda by a foreigner. “You cannot understand India with Italian glasses,” a senior party leader, Tarun Chugh, told the Indian television network NDTV this week.

Image

In a 1981 photo, Sonia Gandhi, left, is accompanied her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, who arrived at Delhi’s airport after winning elections in Amethi. He is flanked by their daughter, Priyanka, and son, Rahul. To the right is the Bollywood star Amitabh Bachchan. Credit...Sondeep Shankar/Getty Images

Beyond the skirmishing, the memoir is remarkable as the journey of the shy young woman who was in the back seat of the car with her bloodied, dying mother-in-law as she was taken to the hospital, and whose life of love, hate, joy and tragedy mirrors the convulsive history of modern India.

## ‘He Was Very Good Looking’

Sonia Gandhi, now a member of the upper house of Parliament, has given very few interviews over nearly 30 years in politics. She was gracious but visibly nervous as she took her place on a sofa in her white-columned bungalow, built in the 1930s by British colonial rulers in the heart of New Delhi. She wore a pink silk sari, had her gray hair pulled back in a headband and spoke softly, and sometimes tentatively, in Italian-accented English. Her daughter, 54, was beside her for what her mother called moral support.

Her book, 12 years in the making, was to have been published by Penguin Random House India. But Manjulika Dubey, Sonia Gandhi’s closest friend, who worked with her on the memoir, said the publisher backed away because of the book’s criticism of the B.J.P. and the far-right Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. Representatives for Penguin Random House said the decision not to move forward was mutual.

The book was published on Tuesday in India and Britain by Harper Collins and in the United States by Knopf.

Sonia Gandhi said she wrote the memoir because her children and Ms. Dubey pestered her to do so. “She’s quite a private person,” Rahul Gandhi said in a telephone interview. “But my sister and I felt that there were things that she had gone through that were important for people to know.”

Yet Mrs. Gandhi does not delve into her political life, which began with her joining the Congress Party in 1997, until nearly 400 pages in. Much of the memoir is about her experiences in the Gandhi household, her complicated relationship with her mother-in-law and her courtship and marriage with Rajiv.

Image

Sonia Gandhi at a table near a bust of Indira Gandhi, her mother-in-law and the former prime minister of India.Credit...Saumya Khandelwal for The New York Times

“That’s the part that I love the most,” she said.

She met him in January 1965 when he was 20 and studying engineering at Trinity College, Cambridge. She was 19 and enrolled at an English language school nearby. She had noticed him in a Greek restaurant — “he was very good looking” she said — and he had noticed her, too. The attraction was so intense that six months later Rajiv insisted that she meet his formidable mother, then a minister in Nehru’s government, who was visiting London.

“I was terrified,” Sonia Gandhi said. When her future mother-in-law asked her about herself, she was so nervous that she burst into tears.

She was married in New Delhi in 1968, two years after Indira Gandhi became prime minister. The young bride moved into the official, bustling household, struggled to learn Hindi and to adjust to Indian food and customs. Rajiv Gandhi, who quit engineering studies to become an airline pilot, was away at flight school. Sometimes it would be just Sonia Gandhi and her mother-in-law at the dining table, where the prime minister would often read a newspaper and ignore her, Sonia Gandhi wrote.

By 1975, Indira Gandhi was facing attacks from the opposition and a conviction on two counts of electoral corruption — the use of the services of a government official and of a rostrum in an election campaign — leading her rivals to demand her resignation. She responded by declaring a state of emergency. She jailed her opponents, suspended India’s equivalent of the bill of rights, censored the press and arrested thousands.

Image

A 1975 photo shows Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declaring India to be in a state of emergency, allowing her to jail her political opponents. Credit...Bettmann

“It was something that should not have been done,” Sonia Gandhi said, carefully.

Indira Gandhi called for elections in 1977, was trounced by the opposition and jailed for a week. Sonia Gandhi brought her food from home. “I was moved to tears seeing her tiny figure sitting on a metal chair in that bare, cold jail cell,” she wrote.

Indira Gandhi was re-elected in January 1980. Five months later, after her younger son and presumed political heir, Sanjay, died in a stunt plane crash, she turned to her elder son to carry on the family name in politics. Sonia Gandhi begged her husband for a year to say no but ultimately, she wrote, “I broke.” Rajiv Gandhi won a seat in Parliament in 1981 and eventually his reluctant wife joined him on trips to his constituency in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.

Image

Rajiv and Sonia Gandhi campaigning in Amethi, Utter Pradesh, in 1981.Credit...Bhawan Singh/The India Today Group, via Getty Images

The next years were violent. In June 1984, Indira Gandhi ordered an army assault on Sikh militants holed up in Punjab’s Golden Temple, the holiest shrine in Sikhism. Hundreds of militants, soldiers and civilians were killed, according to the government, but independent estimates have put the death toll as high as several thousand.

Retaliation was swift. On the morning of Oct. 31, 1984, Sonia Gandhi was about to start her bath when she heard a series of explosions. She ran outside to see that her mother-in-law had been gunned down by two of her Sikh bodyguards as she walked through the garden of her residence. The prime minister was rushed into the back seat of a car. Sonia Gandhi crouched on the floor beside her.

“Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression,” Sonia Gandhi wrote. “She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, ‘Mummy, Mummy,’ but no word comes out.”

Indira Gandhi was declared dead at 2 p.m. Rajiv Gandhi arrived at the hospital soon after with the news that he was to be sworn in as prime minister. “They will kill you too!” Sonia Gandhi burst out. Her husband replied, she wrote, “They will kill me anyway.”

Image

Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, left in a white hat, attended the cremation of his mother, the former prime minister Indira Gandhi, in New Delhi on Nov. 3, 1984. He was joined by his wife Sonia and their daughter, Priyanka. Credit...Bettmann

As the young prime minister embarked on an ambitious modernization program, his wife became a virtual recluse. “I sort of went into myself,” Sonia Gandhi said. “I think I had some

items.title: The United States Is Skipping COP31 in Turkey
items.summary: President Trump refused to send an American delegation to the United Nations climate summit in Turkey.
items.full_text:
Title: The United States Is Skipping COP31 in Turkey - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/climate/trump-cop31-climate-turkey.html

Published Time: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:58:05 GMT

Markdown Content:
As world leaders begin addressing the United Nations climate summit today in Antalya, Turkey, 197 nations will be represented. From Albania to Zimbabwe, heads of state and governments and top ministers will commit to the global goal of a livable planet.

But not the United States.

For the second year in a row, the most powerful country on Earth and the largest contributor of planet-warming emissions in history has refused to participate in the global effort to slow climate change.

President Trump, who called global warming the “greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world,” withdrew the United States from the 2015 Paris climate agreement and stopped sending American delegations to the annual negotiations, known this year as COP31.

The United States is no longer trying to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions, has cut support for scientific research into global warming and halted funding to help vulnerable countries cope with the impacts of climate change.

That’s left the rest of the world scrambling to fill the vacuum.

“Look, whenever the mic was on, and it was the turn of the U.S. to speak, we all listened,” said Yaw Bediako Osafo, a negotiator from Ghana who is leading a group of African countries in the talks. “Now the world’s superpower is pulling out and saying, ‘Well, we’re not going to be involved.’”

The political climate in the United States changed abruptly last week, as Democrats dominated the midterms. The new Congress controlled by Democrats will have limited power to enact climate policies with Mr. Trump still in office. But Democrats said they intend to rein in the Trump administration, which has promoted fossil fuels and waged attacks on the clean energy industry.

“There does seem to be some positive messages coming out of the U.S. recently,” said Tina Stege, the lead negotiator for the Marshall Islands, who’s low-lying atoll country is threatened by rising sea levels.

[54 Democrats Dem. Republicans Rep. 50 44](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-senate.html)[255 Democrats Dem. Republicans Rep. 218 167](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-house.html)

Some are already looking ahead to the possibility that, if a Democrat were elected president in 2028, the United States might return to the U.N. climate negotiations.

“If what was manifested in this election continues, we’re going to elect someone who really wants to get something serious done on climate,” said John Kerry, who served as the U.S. climate envoy in the Biden administration.

Mr. Kerry said he believed other countries would welcome the return of the United States, as long as “there’s no arrogance and there’s a readiness to work.”

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said: “The United States is focused on common sense, not climate nonsense. The Trump Administration will continue to work with our allies around the world to restore energy abundance and unleash affordable, reliable, secure energy sources.”

While China, the world’s largest present-day emitter, leads the world in the manufacturing and export of renewable energy technologies, Beijing has not stepped forward to fill the space vacated by the United States.

Some countries like Britain and Japan have pushed forward with plans to drive down greenhouse gases.

Image

Demonstrators outside the conference on Tuesday.Credit...Murad Sezer/Reuters

And under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Canada has scaled back some of its ambitious climate initiatives over the last year. The country abandoned a federal consumer carbon fuel charge and canceled plans to put a cap on greenhouse gas emissions from the oil and gas sector.

“I don’t see a real clear leader,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the United Nations. “Countries are distracted from what used to be kind of a north star for all of us.”

Several people said when the world’s largest polluter is doubling down on fossil fuels, it makes it easier for other polluting countries to downplay climate change.

“When the U.S. stands up and stands tall and assumes that moral leadership, many things follow,” said Swarnim Waglé, Nepal’s finance minister. “With perceived withdrawal, other countries also retreat.”

Yet some said they were glad the United States was absent. At previous climate summits, the Trump administration had been an impediment to progress, they said. During Mr. Trump’s first term, his administration [promoted coal at the climate talks](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/02/climate/trump-coal-cop23-bonn.html).

“Under this administration it’s better that they’re not here,” said Rachel Cleetus, director of the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “We’ve been such an unreliable partner in this space.”

Still, many Americans are participating at events at COP31, including foundations and nonprofit groups based in the United States as well as current and former Democratic politicians and policymakers.

Gavin Newsom, the California governor and a possible 2028 presidential candidate, is arriving on Thursday, along with Tim Walz, the governor of Minnesota, according to several U.S. officials. Al Gore, the former vice president, is speaking at events on the sidelines.

Gina McCarthy, the White House climate adviser during the Biden administration, is leading a contingent of 120 U.S. officials including mayors, governors and business leaders. About 19 House Democrats also are traveling to Antalya, led by Representative Sean Casten of Illinois.

Ms. McCarthy said her group wanted to send the message that most Americans still care about climate change. She said that message got a little easier to deliver after the midterm election.

“Hopefully, the rest of the world will feel less anxious about whether the U.S. can pull itself out of this administration and get back to the level of work that we all expect,” she said.

Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, planned to attend and said it was important to show up.

“America gets enormous advantages from having a primary and respected role in the international community,” he said. “When we choose not to engage on an important matter like this, we just squander all of those opportunities.”

items.title: Here’s the latest.
items.full_text: U.S. inflation remained elevated last month, underscoring the need for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again this year. Overall prices rose 0.4 percent in October after a 0.6 percent jump in September, according to the latest Consumer Price Index report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. “Core” prices, which strip out volatile food and energy items, rose 0.3 percent. The agency on Tuesday did not release year-over-year figures for October because it was unable to collect data during last year’s government shutdown. According to calculations by The New York Times, overall prices were around 4 percent higher compared with the same time last year, up from 3.7 percent in September. Over the same period, core prices rose about 2.8 percent. One of the biggest drivers of inflation in October was food. Prices rose 0.5 percent last month and about 3 percent since the same time last year. That likely reflects a surge in energy prices, especially diesel prices , which have exploded costs for farmers. Energy prices overall rose modestly in October and were up 0.7 percent for the month after a 5.2 percent jump in September. Gasoline prices rose 1 percent, significantly slower than the 9.1 percent increase during the previous period. Electricity prices rose nearly 1 percent. October’s C.P.I. report was the last before the Fed meets for its final gathering of the year on Dec. 8-9. Policymakers have signaled that they will raise rates next month as they seek to stamp out price pressures that have pushed inflation further from their goal. While the Fed tracks C.P.I., it officially targets 2 percent inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures index. That level has been overshot for nearly six years. Fed officials also watch the price of services as an indicator of the underlying pace of inflation. Specifically, they have been looking at core services excluding housing, a measure sometimes referred to as “supercore.” Those prices rose 0.4 percent in October, and have risen at an annual rate of nearly 5.5 percent over the past three months. On Tuesday, Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor, raised the prospects of a larger-than-usual half-point interest rate increase at the bank’s meeting in December if inflation did not show signs of moderating. In remarks delivered at a Bank of England event, Mr. Waller said a quarter-point increase would suffice if price pressures improved. But if “core” inflation rose 0.3 percent or more, as October’s data showed, Mr. Waller warned that the Fed risked its credibility by not moving more aggressively. “Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” he said. Two-year Treasury yields, which are sensitive to changes in interest rate expectations, were up over 0.1 percentage points on Tuesday to 4.67 percent as investors raised wagers that the Fed would raise rates more over time to quell inflation. The labor market remains in solid shape , as October’s report released on Friday showed, affirming that the Fed can focus solely on its inflation problem. October marked the seventh straight month in which price increases outpaced wage growth on a 12-month basis. Average hourly earnings were up 3.1 percent in October from a year earlier, well below the roughly 4 percent annual inflation pace. Show more Nov. 10, 2026, 12:25 p.m. ET Real estate equity held by Americans has soared to about $36 trillion as of September, from around $18 trillion in 2019. Credit... Steve Dipaola/Reuters The latest report on overall household debt and credit by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York shows that U.S. households remain in decent financial health. But there are still major splits between Americans who own homes and large stock portfolios and lower-income segments of the population, according to the data, which was released on Tuesday, and recent reports from private banks. The report from the New York Fed showed that mortgage debt balances rose by $257 billion from July to September, totaling $13.4 trillion. That’s a strikingly large amount of debt, but the vast majority of Americans are managing to service it. The stabilizing power of the 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage continues to be the strongest anchor for households’ finances. After a surge in home buying during the pandemic, tens of millions of families are still benefiting from having locked in low-rate monthly payments. That has served as a meaningful buffer for consumers, even as overall inflation has eroded their purchasing power more broadly in recent years. Another sign of underlying resilience can be found in home equity lines of credit, which are revolving loans backed by the value of the borrowers’ home. They tend to carry much lower interest rates than credit cards, and they allow borrowers to tap their wealth without selling their home. HELOC balances rose by $23 billion in the third quarter of the year, the 18th consecutive quarterly gain, and the largest increase since 2005. Affluent and upper middle-class households in particular have been using HELOCs in recent years for home repairs and renovations, as well as for personal expenses. Unlike 2005, when the housing bubble was near its peak, Fed researchers note that this borrowing now seems to largely be stemming from strength — not stress. Serious delinquency for these lines of credit is exceptionally low, hovering around 1 percent. Homeowners’ equity in real estate has soared to about $36 trillion as of September from around $18 trillion in 2019. Real estate wealth is unequally distributed in the United States, with the top 10 percent of households constituting a disproportionate share of household net worth. The surge in HELOCs made sense in view of that data, the New York Fed researchers wrote, the calling these loans “a logical point for extracting that equity.” Still, households that are current on their debt payments are not necessarily comfortable. Other Federal Reserve research in recent years has shown that about 40 percent of the population has “little to no disposable income” at the end of month, after taxes and basic expenses are met. Credit cards borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores are now showing higher levels of distress, according to the New York Fed, while higher-income consumers have generally avoided a deterioration in credit. And this month, a team of researchers at Bank of America noted, using anonymized account data, that financial pressure is extending beyond lower-income households. Lower-to-middle income renters are perennially stretched, but around one in four higher-income mortgage holders are also spending more than half their income on housing, according to the bank. Financial experts generally recommend that consumers should spend no more than 30 percent of their monthly income on housing costs. With interest rates elevated, and prices much higher for new vehicles than just a few years ago, auto loan payments have become a point of stress for lower-income borrowers as well — even if many are still finding ways to budget and meet their monthly obligations. In a bright spot, student loan debt delinquencies have moderated. When Biden-era federal aid for those deep in student loan debt was reversed last year, there were widespread fears among some analysts that a burst in defaults could occur. For now, though, it appears most borrowers have been able to stave off missed student-loan payments. Show more
